reasoning: The core problem — whether legibility benefits depend on the verifier's capability and shrink as the verifier weakens relative to the prover — is substantially covered by existing published work. OpenAI's Prover-Verifier Games (Kirchner et al. 2024, 2407.13692) already uses GSM8K with helpful (legible-correct) and sneaky (plausible-incorrect) provers, measures small/weak verifier accept-reject accuracy, and explicitly finds a capability-relative effect (medium-sized verifiers ~3x10^-3 of the prover benefit most, while both smaller and larger verifiers benefit less), and that legibility transfers to smaller verifiers and humans. The very recent "Measuring Weak-to-Strong Legibility of Reasoning Models" (2603.20508) goes further, introducing "transfer utility" for how useful traces are to weaker models and extending it to verifying strong models, finding verifier accuracy is predicted by prover transfer utility — essentially the proposed question. Scalable-oversight work (2407.04622, "Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight") and "When to Trust the Cheap Check" (2602.17633) further document judge/verifier accuracy degrading with the judge-prover capability gap. The one genuinely unexplored slice is the clean, dedicated, inference-only ablation contrasting fixed legible-correct vs terse-correct vs sneaky-incorrect solutions across a deliberately ordered ladder of weakening open verifiers to chart how the legible-minus-terse advantage curve evolves — a specific measurement framing not exactly reproduced in any single source, which keeps this short of already_solved.

evidence.title: Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility of LLM outputs (Kirchner et al., 2024)
evidence.summary: Foundational paper: GSM8K, helpful (legible-correct) and sneaky (plausible-incorrect) provers, small/weak verifier accept-reject training. Finds legibility transfers to smaller verifiers and time-constrained humans, and that medium-sized verifiers (~3x10^-3 of prover) benefit most while smaller and larger verifiers benefit less — a capability-relative legibility effect directly overlapping the proposed question.

evidence.title: Measuring Weak-to-Strong Legibility of Reasoning Models (2026)
evidence.summary: Introduces 'transfer utility' measuring how useful a model's reasoning traces are to weaker, non-reasoning models, evaluated over 90k traces from 12 reasoning models. Extends this to verifying correctness of strong models, finding verifier accuracy (precision of flagged traces) is predicted by the prover's transfer utility — nearly the exact question of whether legibility benefit depends on verifier capability.

evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs (DeepMind, 2024)
evidence.summary: Empirically studies weaker LLM judges evaluating stronger LLMs across protocols (debate, consultancy). Finds judge accuracy degrades as agent capability increases relative to the judge — the capability-gap dependence of verification accuracy central to the proposal.

evidence.title: When to Trust the Cheap Check: Weak and Strong Verification for Reasoning (2026)
evidence.summary: Studies weak vs strong verifier performance gaps, finding the gap narrows on easier problems (weak verifiers reliably recognize correct responses when problems are easy). Directly characterizes how verification accuracy varies with verifier strength.

evidence.title: Mitigating Legibility Tax with Decoupled Prover-Verifier Games (2026)
evidence.summary: Names and analyzes the 'legibility tax' (accuracy degradation from legibility training) and proposes a decoupled translator-based framework, confirming the legibility-tax framing the proposal builds on is an active, recently treated topic.

evidence.title: Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight
evidence.summary: Community work modeling how oversight/verification success depends on the capability ratio between overseer and overseen model, providing a theoretical frame for the proposed empirical ladder of weakening verifiers.
